title: Higher-Order Interactions in Complex Systems: Mechanisms, Behaviour, Representation and Reducibility
abstract: Higher-order interactions couple three or more elements in ways that cannot be decomposed into pairwise contributions. In diverse complex systems they produce striking collective behaviours such as explosive synchronization, discontinuous transitions and altered stability. Neither such behaviour nor a description written in many-body terms establishes a many-body mechanism, since both depend on how the system is represented. This review distinguishes three questions: what mechanism governs the system, what behaviour does it produce, and how is either represented? Representation covers both which variables are included and how relations among them are encoded. We examine direct many-body mechanisms, nonlinear but pairwise mechanisms that mimic them, and indirect routes through shared environments or eliminated variables, together with temporal aggregation, an artefact of observation rather than a mechanism. The same behaviour can arise from different mechanisms, and a given higher-order mechanism has no universal behavioural consequence. We then formulate reducibility, the question of whether a higher-order model can be replaced by a lower-order one, as a comparison between a source model and an admissible class of lower-order models, relative to a target and a tolerance. The target may be a microscopic rule, an observable or a qualitative feature. Information-theoretic and inferential methods are reviewed as complementary tools for detecting higher-order dependence, testing lower-order alternatives and reconstructing interaction structure. However, observational data alone generally cannot establish the mechanism. We close by identifying open problems in linking mechanisms to measurable signatures, coarse-graining, identifiability and causality, and in extending reductions beyond mean field. (Abridged)
summary: This review provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for analyzing higher-order interactions in complex systems, separating the concepts of mechanism, observable behavior, and mathematical representation. It argues that these three aspects are not equivalent, demonstrating that observed collective phenomena can arise from multiple underlying physical causes. The work establishes formal criteria for determining when a complex, high-order model can be accurately simplified or reduced to a lower-order description.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a unified framework for understanding higher-order interactions in complex systems by rigorously distinguishing between the underlying physical mechanism, the resulting observable behavior, and the mathematical representation used to describe them.
main_result: The core finding is that observed collective behavior does not uniquely determine the underlying mechanism, as the same behavior can arise from different mechanisms or through mere representational artifacts.
method: The review employs conceptual analysis, drawing distinctions between mechanistic, statistical, and representational definitions, and formalizing the concept of 'reducibility' by comparing source models to admissible lower-order approximations.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to general complex systems, including coupled oscillators (like the Kuramoto model), ecological communities, and neural networks, which are modeled using generalized Hamiltonians or non-equilibrium equations of motion containing higher-order coupling terms.
key_observables: Collective behaviors such as explosive synchronization, discontinuous phase transitions, and altered stability regimes.
important_parameters: The order of interaction (pairwise vs. higher-order), the target of reduction (microscopic rule vs. observable feature), and the tolerance level for approximation.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation noted is that observational data alone is generally insufficient to uniquely establish the true underlying mechanism.
figures_summary: Figure 1 conceptually structures the relationship between mechanisms, behavior, and representation, while the notes imply tables summarizing the formalisms for defining higher-order interactions.
paper_structure: The paper is structured around distinguishing three core questions: what governs the system (mechanism), what does it produce (behavior), and how is it described (representation). It then formalizes the concept of reducibility and reviews information-theoretic tools for detection.
why_interesting: Although focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous framework for distinguishing mechanism from observation, and the formal treatment of reducibility, provides powerful conceptual tools applicable to open quantum systems where distinguishing between true quantum correlations and classical approximations is paramount.

Any such mechanism, and the behaviour it generates, is expressed within a representation, comprising the structural representation, how the relations among variables are encoded, and the variable representation, which variables the description includes.
